title: Catabolism of Carbon Skeletons of Amino Acids
objectives: Classify amino acids based on their metabolic fates
Describe the conversion of α-ketoacids to major metabolic intermediates
Understand inborn errors of amino acid metabolism
Explain clinical manifestations and management of metabolic disorders

classification.title: Amino Acid Classification
classification.content:
Metabolic Classification

Amino acids are classified based on their α-ketoacid fates:

  • Glucogenic: Yield glucose precursors (OAA, α-KG, etc.)
  • Ketogenic: Yield acetyl-CoA/acetoacetate
  • Both: Can enter both pathways

Key Intermediates

  • Oxaloacetate (OAA)
  • α-Ketoglutarate (α-KG)
  • Fumarate
  • Succinyl-CoA
  • Pyruvate
  • Acetyl-CoA

oxaloacetate.title: Amino Acids Yielding OAA
oxaloacetate.content:
Oxaloacetate Producers

Asparagine (N) & Aspartate (D)

  • Aspartate transaminates with pyruvate → OAA + alanine
  • OAA converted to malate (cytosolic MDH)
  • Malate enters mitochondria via shuttle
  • No known metabolic defects

ketoglutarate.title: Amino Acids Yielding α-KG
ketoglutarate.content:
α-Ketoglutarate Producers

1. Glutamine (Q) & Glutamate (E)

  • Glutaminase: Gln → Glu + NH3
  • Glu → α-KG via GDH or transamination
  • No known defects

2. Arginine (R)

  • Arginase → ornithine
  • Ornithine → glutamate-γ-semialdehyde → Glu
  • Defect: Ornithine transaminase deficiency causes gyrate atrophy

3. Proline (P)

  • Proline → Δ1-pyrroline-5-carboxylate → Glu
  • Hyperprolinemia:
    • Type I: Proline dehydrogenase defect
    • Type II: Glutamate-γ-semialdehyde DH defect

4. Histidine (H)

  • Histidase → urocanate → N-formiminoglutamate (FIGLU)
  • FIGLU + THF → glutamate
  • Histidase deficiency: Benign, elevated histidine/metabolites
  • FIGLU excretion indicates folate deficiency

fumarate.title: Amino Acids Yielding Fumarate
fumarate.content:
Fumarate Producers

Phenylalanine (F) & Tyrosine (Y)

  • Precursors of dopamine, norepinephrine, melanin, thyroxine
  • Both yield fumarate + acetoacetate

Phenylketonuria (PKU)

Types

  • Type I: Phenylalanine hydroxylase defect (classic)
  • Types II/III: DHB reductase defects
  • Types IV/V: DHB biosynthesis defects

Pathology

  • Phe → phenylpyruvate → phenyllactate/phenylacetate
  • Musty urine odor (phenylacetate)
  • Mental retardation from neurotransmitter deficiency

Management

  • Low-Phe diet
  • L-dopa & 5-HTP supplementation
  • Newborn screening (TMS/FeCl3 test)

Tyrosine Disorders

Tyrosinemias

  • Type I: Fumarylacetoacetate hydrolase defect
  • Type II: Tyrosine transaminase defect
  • Type III: p-Hydroxyphenylpyruvate hydroxylase defect

Alkaptonuria

  • Homogentisate oxidase defect
  • Black urine (oxidized homogentisate)
  • Ochronosis & arthritis
  • Treatment: Low Tyr/Phe diet

faqs.title: FAQs
faqs.content:
FAQs

Q: Why does PKU cause mental retardation? +

A: Excess phenylalanine competes with tyrosine/tryptophan transport across BBB, reducing dopamine/serotonin synthesis. It also inhibits glycolysis, depriving the brain of energy.

Q: How does folate deficiency relate to histidine metabolism? +

A: THF is required to accept FIGLU's formimino group. Without folate, FIGLU accumulates and is excreted - a diagnostic marker.

Q: Why does alkaptonuria cause joint problems? +

A: Oxidized homogentisate forms benzoquinoneacetate that binds to connective tissues, causing ochronosis (pigmentation) and degenerative arthritis.
